**Bottom line:** do this if you want a head start on day 1. Nothing here is marked, recorded or required, and you can
skip any part. The course teaches everything again, live. Reading a block explorer is not in the primer: it is taught on
day 1.

The primer is six short parts: five you click through in your browser, and one short run of slides. Every part opens
from the links below, and nothing needs installing.

## The plan

The times are estimates. They will be checked with test students and changed to match.

| # | Part | What you do | Time |
|---|------|-------------|------|
| 1 | [Hashing](#hashing) | Type text, watch its hash | 15 min |
| 2 | [A tamper-evident ledger](#a-tamper-evident-ledger) | Edit one record, see what breaks | 15 min |
| 3 | [Keys and signatures](#keys-and-signatures) | Sign, tamper, use the wrong key, derive an address | 30 min |
| 4 | [Distributed systems](#distributed-systems) | Compare one hub with a peer-to-peer network | 15 min |
| 5 | [Proof-of-work mining](#proof-of-work-mining) | Race the simulated miners | 15 min |
| 6 | [From click to confirmed transaction](#from-click-to-confirmed-transaction) | Nine slides | 30 min |
|   | **Total** | | **about 2 h** |

Take the parts in this order: each uses ideas from the one before.

## Hashing

[Open the hash lab](assets/labs/micro-hashing/){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint. The lab lets you pick the algorithm; use SHA-256, the
hash Bitcoin uses
[@nationalinstituteofstandardsandtechnologyus_securehashstandard_2015; @nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008].
The lab also offers MD5, SHA-1 and a toy hash, so you can compare. SHA-1 has had a real collision found
[@stevens_firstcollisionfull_2017].

Try this:

1. Set *Algorithm* to SHA-256. Pick the avalanche demo `"HELLO" vs "HELLo"` and read the two hashes. Red marks show
   where they differ. How much of the hash changed for a one-letter change?
2. Type your own text in *Input A* and the same text in *Input B*. What do you get? Change one character in *Input B*.
3. Pick the built-in MD5 collision demo. The lab switches to MD5 and shows two different inputs with the same hash,
   marked "collision". The lab labels MD5 "broken" for this reason. Switch back to SHA-256 afterwards.
4. Press *Start* under *Uniform Distribution Demo*. Watch the counts spread across the bars.

**You are done when** you can say why a hash works as a fingerprint of data.

## A tamper-evident ledger

[Open the ledger lab](assets/labs/tamper-ledger/tamper_ledger_lab.html){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

In a blockchain, each block carries the hash of the block before it
[@nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008]. The lab builds a small ledger of deposits and transfers between three
wallets so you can see why that chain of hashes exposes an edit. Its hash is a short toy hash, not SHA-256; the linking
idea is the same.

Try this:

1. Add three or four transactions with *Add Transaction*. The ledger says "Chain valid".
2. Click into the text of an early entry and change one digit of the amount, then press Tab or click away. What does the ledger say now, and what happened to the
   wallet balances?
3. Press *Rehash* on that entry to hide your edit. Which entry now shows a problem? Keep going. How many entries must you
   fix to cover one change?
4. Read the *Event Log* to see each step.

**You are done when** you can explain why editing an old record is visible to everyone holding a copy.

## Keys and signatures

[Open the signatures lab](assets/labs/signatures/){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

A digital signature lets anyone check that a message came from the holder of a private key, and that the message was
not changed. A wallet signs a transaction this way [@antonopoulos_masteringethereum_2018].

Try this, in order:

1. **Sign.** Keep the default algorithm (ECDSA P-256). Press *Generate Key Pair*, then *Sign with Private Key*. Press *Use Signer's Key* and then *Verify with
   Public Key*. The lab says the signature is valid.
2. **Tamper.** Press *Flip 1 Hex Digit* on the signature, or change one word of the message, and verify again. What does
   the lab say? Press *Restore* to undo the signature change.
3. **Wrong key.** Press *Generate Wrong Key* and verify the original signature again. Why does it fail?
4. **Address derivation.** In the *Address Derivation* panel, press *Derive Address*; it uses the key pair you made.
   Read the three derivation steps beneath it.

**One difference from day 1.** This lab signs with P-256 or Ed25519 (and RSA), through your browser. Bitcoin, Ethereum
and Tron all use a different curve, **secp256k1** (as of 24 Oct 2026)
[@certicom_sec2recommendedelliptic_2010; @antonopoulos_masteringbitcoinprogramming_2017; @antonopoulos_masteringethereum_2018; @tron_accounts_2026].
Day 1 teaches secp256k1 and the real address formats. The address you derive here is a teaching model, not a
usable Bitcoin address, so do not compare it with one.

The lab holds three more panels that are off target for this course: key agreement (ECDH), a curve plot and a nonce-reuse
demo. They are hidden. Instructors can show them by adding `?full` to the lab's address.

**You are done when** you can say what the private key does, what the public key does, and why the wrong key or an
edited message fails verification.

If the key boxes show a line starting `mode=toy`, the lab is using a simple stand-in for real signatures, because the
page was opened over plain HTTP (browsers switch real signing off on an insecure address). The steps work the same way.
For real browser signatures, open the course site's HTTPS address or the lab on `localhost`.

## Distributed systems

[Open the network lab](assets/labs/distributed-systems/distributed_systems_lab.html){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

Bitcoin runs on a peer-to-peer network rather than on one central server [@nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008].
The lab sets the two designs side by side.

Try this:

1. Press *Start Transaction Propagation* and compare the *Hops* count of each design when every node has the transaction.
2. Press *Reset*, then press *Simulate Node Failure* several times. What happens to the centralized network when the hub fails? What happens
   to the peer-to-peer network?
3. Read the two *Trade-offs* boxes under the simulation.

**You are done when** you can name one thing a central hub does better and one thing a peer-to-peer network does better.

## Proof-of-work mining

[Open the mining simulator](assets/labs/POW_mining_micro/){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

In proof of work, miners compete to find a number whose hash meets a target; the first to find one adds the next block,
and the network adjusts the difficulty to keep blocks arriving at a steady pace
[@nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008]. The simulator is a game version: instead of hashes, each miner flips
virtual coins and tries to match a target pattern of heads and tails. You play against five simulated miners.

Try this:

1. On *Level 1*, press *Start Game*, then press *Mine Now* until someone matches the target. Did you or a bot win? How
   many attempts did it take?
2. Play again. Raise the number of nodes or the rate. Who wins more often?
3. Open *Level 2*. Press *Start Level 2* and keep mining. Every four blocks the game compares the average block time with
   the target and changes the difficulty (the number of flips to match). Watch what happens to the difficulty when blocks
   come too fast.

**You are done when** you can say what a miner is searching for, why more computing power wins more often, and why the
network changes the difficulty.

## From click to confirmed transaction

Last, nine slides from the course's closing lesson, "Blockchain in the Real World". They follow one payment from a
user's click to a recorded transaction, and name each piece in the path: wallet, RPC provider, node, chain
[@antonopoulos_masteringethereum_2018; @ethereumorg_transactions_2025].

Open the first link below, then press the right arrow seven times to reach the eighth slide. The ninth slide sits
further on in the deck, so it has its own link. Stop after it; the rest of the deck is for later in the course. Each
link also opens its own slide.

1. [What does a user actually interact with?](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/what-does-a-user-actually-interact-with)
2. [Walking a transaction step by step](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/walking-a-transaction-step-by-step)
3. [Wallets: the control layer](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/wallets-the-control-layer)
4. [Custody models](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/custody-models)
5. [What users actually do](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/what-users-actually-do)
6. [RPC providers: the access layer](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/rpc-providers-the-access-layer)
7. [Nodes and validators](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/nodes-and-validators)
8. [The full blockchain system](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/the-full-blockchain-system)
9. [Bridges: linking separate chains](lessons/conclusion/01-AS-blockchain_in_the_real_world.html#/bridges-linking-separate-chains)

The ninth slide is only the basics: blockchains do not share assets with each other, so a bridge locks a token on one
chain and issues a linked copy on another, which adds trust and security risk [@l31_ethereumorg_blockchainbridges_2026].

**You are done when** you can say, in your own words, what happens between pressing *send* and the transaction being
recorded.

## What happens next

Day 1 starts from these ideas and goes further: blocks and chains, keys on secp256k1, addresses, and reading a real
transaction in an explorer. Bring any question the primer raised.
